summary: TLS 1.3 is widely used and offers better security and privacy than TLS 1.2, so new protocols that use TLS must require TLS 1.3. This best current practice does not apply to DTLS, because DTLS 1.3 is not yet widely deployed. It updates RFC 9325.

eli5.summary: If a new club is being started, it should only accept the newest, safest membership card. Older cards still work for old clubs, but new clubs should not take them.

subtitle: New protocols that use TLS must make TLS 1.3 their default, and TLS 1.2 becomes an optional extra.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.2 can be configured securely, but it takes bespoke configuration, and some weaknesses (such as unencrypted handshake content) cannot be configured away.
tldr.mechanism: Any new protocol that uses TLS MUST specify TLS 1.3 as its default. It MAY allow TLS 1.2 only as an additional, non-default option. The rule covers TLS only, not DTLS.
tldr.outcome: This BCP updates RFC 9325, turning TLS 1.3 from SHOULD into MUST for new protocols and TLS 1.2 from MUST into MAY.

today: RFC 9852 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2026. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 9325.

sections.title: What the RFC Requires
sections.content:
RFC 9852 says that new protocols that use TLS must assume that TLS 1.3 is available and require its use. The rule pertains to TLS only. It does not pertain to DTLS in any version, because DTLS 1.3 is not widely available or deployed.

The RFC describes TLS 1.3 as being in widespread use. It encrypts more of the traffic so that outsiders cannot read it, removes most cryptographic primitives now considered weak, and has had comprehensive security proofs. TLS 1.2 is still in use and can be configured to be secure, but addressing its deficiencies usually requires bespoke configuration.
sections.eli5: New things built on TLS should use the newest version, TLS 1.3, because it is safer without extra fiddling. This rule is only for TLS, not for its cousin DTLS.

sections.title: The Rule for New Protocols
sections.content:
Any new protocol that uses TLS MUST specify TLS 1.3 as its default. As an example, QUIC requires TLS 1.3 and says endpoints MUST terminate the connection if an older version is used.

If deployment considerations are a concern, the protocol MAY specify TLS 1.2 as an additional, non-default option. The RFC gives a counter example: the usage profile for DNS over TLS makes TLS 1.2 the default while also allowing TLS 1.3. Newer specifications that choose to support TLS 1.2 are to reverse those preferences.
sections.eli5: A new protocol must pick TLS 1.3 as the normal way to connect. If some people truly cannot upgrade, the older version may be allowed as a backup, but never as the first choice.

sections.title: Version Negotiation
sections.content:
In the initial TLS handshake, a client says which versions of TLS it supports, and the server is intended to pick the highest version that it also supports. This is called TLS version negotiation. Many TLS libraries let an application specify a range of versions, including an open interval where only the lowest or highest version is given.

If the application uses a TLS implementation that supports version negotiation, and it knows the implementation will use the highest version supported, clients SHOULD specify just the minimum version they want. That minimum MUST be TLS 1.3 or TLS 1.2, depending on whether the protocol allows the older version.
sections.eli5: When two computers meet, the client lists the versions it knows and the server picks the newest one they share. The client only needs to say the oldest version it will accept.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 9325
sections.content:
RFC 9325 gives recommendations for deployed services that use TLS and DTLS. It calls TLS 1.3 widely available, and the move to TLS 1.3 has grown since it was published. RFC 9852 therefore makes two changes to Section 3.1.1 of that document, for TLS only:

  • TLS 1.3 was a SHOULD; for new protocols using TLS it is now a MUST.
  • TLS 1.2 was a MUST; it is now a MAY, as described in the rule above.
sections.eli5: An older rulebook said the new card should be used if possible and the old card was required. Now it is flipped: the new card is required for new clubs and the old card is optional.

sections.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
sections.content:
Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs), once available, will have a huge impact on TLS traffic. To mitigate this, TLS applications will need to migrate to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). The RFC leaves aside when an application actually needs PQC.

It does note that the TLS Working Group is focusing its efforts on TLS 1.3 or later, and that TLS 1.2 will not be supported (see RFC 9851). PQC is actively being standardized for TLS 1.3, so requiring TLS 1.3 gives new applications the option to use it.
sections.eli5: One day very powerful computers may be able to crack today's secret codes. The new codes are being built for TLS 1.3, so a new protocol that uses TLS 1.3 can switch to them later.

sections.title: Why TLS 1.2 Falls Short
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that TLS 1.2 can be configured securely; it is just much harder than using TLS 1.3. It lists several weaknesses.

  • Renegotiation attacks and the Triple Handshake attack, which let an attacker inject a chosen prefix into the plaintext stream. Securing TLS 1.2 means disabling renegotiation or using the extension in RFC 5746.
  • Key exchange: RSA key exchange and finite field Diffie-Hellman have weaknesses, and most of these methods must be disabled (see RFC 10015).
  • Ciphers: RC4 has exploitable key stream biases, and CBC cipher suites have been a source of vulnerabilities, including the Lucky13 timing attack.
  • Other attacks that TLS 1.3 is immune to: BEAST, Logjam, FREAK and SLOTH.
  • Privacy: in TLS 1.2 most of the content of the handshake messages is not encrypted. This is a protocol issue that cannot be fixed by configuration.
sections.eli5: The old version can be made safe, but it is like a lock with many tricky settings, and some parts of it show your business to onlookers no matter what. The new version is safer by default.
